problem: Navigation world models (e.g. NWM) predict future egocentric views but are only prediction modules; they need an external CEM-style planner to sample, score and select actions, which is costly and makes closed-loop behavior depend on planning choices. Direct navigation policies are efficient but are not trained to predict the visual consequences of their actions.
motivation: Under partial observability a robot must anticipate how motion changes its view and whether that brings it closer to the goal. The paper asks how explicit visual foresight can be made directly usable for closed-loop control without test-time search, by learning it jointly with the action and value targets that determine behavior.
key_idea: Fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion transformer (Cosmos Predict2) to jointly denoise a shared latent canvas holding the action chunk, future state, future egocentric views and a goal-progress value, so that one forward denoising pass yields an executable action plus foresight.
insight: Future-image prediction alone plus CEM is insufficient: image-only with CEM (N=120) gives ATE 0.326/0.569 at h=4/8, versus 0.107/0.287 after adding action and state supervision, and 0.076/0.192 after adding value. Removing the future-image loss in the full model hurts (ATE 0.262 vs 0.192 at h=8), so foresight, action and value supervision are complementary and the joint formulation is what makes foresight useful. CEM accuracy for NWM saturates from N=8 and does not close the gap to single-pass NavWAM.
method: World-action latent canvas: fixed 9-frame latent sequence; observed frames are a blank pad, current state, goal image and current observation; generated frames are the action chunk, future state, two future observations (o_{t+H-1}, o_{t+H}) and a goal-progress value.

Backbone: Cosmos-Predict2 2B Video2World (causal VAE + DiT); non-image variables (state, action, value) are normalized, broadcast over the latent spatial grid and decoded by spatial averaging, with no separate heads.
Training objective: a single rectified-flow denoising loss on generated frames, with the action frame upweighted (lambda=5).
Multi-mode conditioning: policy / world-model / value modes sampled 50/25/25 per sample, so one set of weights does action generation, action-conditioned prediction and value estimation.
Goal-progress value: v = clip(1 - ||p_end - p_t|| / d_max, 0, 1); a geodesic version is used for HM3D.
Inference: policy mode only, a single denoising chain gives an action chunk (H=4) executed receding-horizon at about 5 Hz; optional value-guided best-of-N is not used in the reported results.
Three-phase curriculum: HM3D simulator pretrain (H=16, 802 scenes / 185k trajectories), joint fine-tune on RECON/SACSON/SCAND (H=4), optional per-dataset fine-tune on GO Stanford.

setting.training_data: Phase 1: HM3D simulator trajectories (802 scenes, 185k trajectories) generated by the authors' navigation policy; Phase 2: RECON (11,835), SACSON (2,000), SCAND (372) trajectories; Phase 3 (w/ FT): GO Stanford (3,544 trajectories)
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB 224x224 plus goal image and robot state (x, y, yaw)
setting.action_space: predicted local-frame waypoint increments (dx, dy, dyaw), chunk H=4, executed as cmd_vel
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D pretraining only); evaluation is on offline datasets and a real robot
setting.privileged: none at test time (state pose is an input; the value label uses GT trajectory metadata only in training)

numbers_note: No standard VLN/ObjNav benchmark reported. Results are on GO Stanford, SIT and a real-world test with custom metrics (ATE/RPE); Table 1 does not state a horizon, and the h=8 values match it.
results: Without CEM search, NavWAM reduces ATE from 0.453 (NWM) and 0.455 (Cosmos Predict2 + CEM) to 0.324 zero-shot and 0.192 with fine-tuning on GO Stanford. It is slightly better than OmniVLA (7B) on SIT (ATE 0.144 vs 0.162 at h=8). In the real world, its success rate is 79.2% versus 58.3% for OmniVLA and 16.7% for NWM, at about 205 ms per action versus about 234 s for NWM with N=120.
limitations: Only image-goal navigation in static indoor scenes is evaluated; language and object goals, dynamic obstacles and long-horizon navigation are untested.
The real-world study is small (24 episodes, one robot); failures come from pose drift and degraded foresight near obstacles.
Inference is dominated by a multi-step diffusion chain (about 5 Hz); the optional best-of-N mode and value calibration are not studied.
